content: Joint stiffness can manifest in several ways. It may refer to the sensation of pain experienced when moving a joint, the subjective perception of a reduced range of motion, or the objective physical finding of a diminished range of motion during a clinical examination. While patients often describe joint stiffness as pain during movement, medical professionals typically use the term to refer to the latter two definitions. Pain during joint movement is frequently caused by osteoarthritis, even in mild cases, as well as other forms of arthritis. It can also result from joint injury, repetitive overuse, or, in rare cases, more serious conditions such as infections or neoplasms. In these instances, the range of motion may remain normal or be restricted due to pain. When a patient reports a loss of motion, they are describing a subjective symptom where they notice that one or more joints no longer move as freely or as far as they previously could or as they need to. This symptom is often associated with more advanced stages of arthritis, including osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis. On the other hand, a loss of range of motion observed during a clinical examination is considered a physical sign. In this case, the healthcare provider, such as an orthopedic surgeon or rheumatologist, identifies that the joint's range of motion is objectively reduced compared to normal values or the unaffected side. The causes of this physical sign are similar to those of the symptom. In severe cases, when a joint becomes completely immobile, it is referred to as ankylosis. Morning stiffness is a hallmark feature of rheumatoid arthritis. If it persists for more than one hour, it indicates significant joint inflammation. Morning stiffness is characterized by difficulty or slowness in moving the joints upon waking or after prolonged periods of inactivity. It typically affects both sides of the body symmetrically and tends to improve with movement.
